name: Diego Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground at Kestrel Deep, a gold mine. People call it an LHD, load-haul-dump: a big low machine with a bucket that scoops the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass, which is a shaft that drops it down to the crusher. Seven hundred metres down, headlights and fans and a radio, ten hours a shift. I love it when a stope, that's an underground room we're mining out, comes clean and the numbers on the board look good. What gets me is the heat in summer and the waiting, because you can't go back in after a blast until the air clears.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the crew like down there, and has the machinery changed since you started?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good crew. Petra and I have run the same level for six years, and Kwame, the shift boss, still brings his mother's flatbread on Fridays. The big change is tele-remote. Some loaders can now be driven from a chair up on the surface with screens and joysticks, and I've done two shifts in that chair. Felt like playing a game with a very expensive controller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe they'll spend money on ventilation instead of gadgets. At work we'd joke about it at crib. Online I might share a news story, but I don't really argue with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think much changes for me, because the remote loaders were coming anyway and they don't need clever AI. The chair on the surface is just cameras and a joystick. So the plateau doesn't protect my seat underground, it just slows the extra stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month aside like now and keep asking for more shifts in the remote chair, because that's where it's heading regardless. Ana's nursing pay and mine cover the house fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit like being told the storm went the other way, but you still need to fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep asking for remote shifts. Why, if nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched how it goes. First it's one loader on remote, then three, then they need fewer of us underground. If I'm already good in the chair when they pick who stays, that's me looking after my family. Nothing clever about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually use AI for now, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked one to explain my payslip when the overtime rate changed, and Sofia uses it for her maths, which I'm not sure about. I don't trust it with anything important yet.

S0.say: I'd say good, maybe now they'll spend money on ventilation instead of gadgets. I'd joke about it at work and maybe share a news story, but I don't argue with strangers online.
S0.think: I don't think much changes for me, because the remote loaders don't need clever AI anyway. The plateau doesn't protect my seat underground, it just slows down the extras.
S0.do: Keeps saving a few hundred a month as he does now. Keeps asking for more shifts in the surface remote-control chair so he's already good at it when the company decides who stays.
S0.feel: Calm, with a sense that the roof still needs fixing even if the storm has passed.
S0.quote: If I'm already good in the chair when they pick who stays, that's me looking after my family.
S0.fieldNote: Diego separates hype about AI from the remote loaders he already uses, and he sees the second as the real change. His plan is quietly positional: be good in the chair before the decision is made. He is relaxed about money because two solid incomes cover the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the union meeting: fine, change is coming, but the company should pay for the training and nobody gets dropped without a plan. And the government should make that the rule for every mine, not leave it to whether the manager is a decent person. I'd post that one, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in the middle. The remote room at Kestrel has eight chairs and there are about thirty of us driving loaders. I'm not the best in the chair, but I'm not the worst, so it's maybe a coin toss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the company's tele-remote course in the first month and do the certificate properly. I'd talk to the union about a rule that remote seats go by seniority and training, not by who the boss likes. And I'd start using the AI tools a bit more, the ones the company puts on the tablets for logging faults, so I'm not the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, because the money's fine and there are three other mines within an hour, but I don't like coin tosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three other mines nearby. Would you go to one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost the coin toss, yes, I'd look. But they'll all be doing the same thing a year or two later. Moving mines buys time, it doesn't fix anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra, funnily enough, even though she's better on the loader than me. She hates screens. She'd rather quit than sit in that room, and she says it out loud in front of the supervisors, which doesn't help her.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming, so the company should pay for training and nobody gets dropped without a plan. The government should make that the rule for every mine, not leave it to whether the manager is decent.
S1.think: I think I'm in the middle: eight remote chairs and about thirty loader drivers. I'm not the best in the chair or the worst, so it's maybe a coin toss.
S1.do: Signs up for the company's tele-remote certificate in the first month and uses the fault-logging AI on the tablets more often. Pushes the union for a rule that remote seats go by seniority and training.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not panicking, because the money is fine and there are other mines nearby.
S1.quote: Moving mines buys time, it doesn't fix anything.
S1.fieldNote: Diego reasons in numbers: eight chairs, thirty drivers. His progressive views show up as a demand for rules that don't depend on a decent manager. He worries for a more skilled colleague whose dislike of screens could cost her, which shows he sees adaptability as the real dividing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has failed if it lets this land with two years' notice and no plan. I'd be at the union meeting saying we need income support for every miner, now, not after. And I'd post that, and I'd go to the march if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the remote chair stops mattering. If AI can do anything a person can do, it drives the loader itself and the eight chairs become one person watching. So my two years of being good in the chair counts for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the plan to build on our block of land and keep the cash. We'd cut the extra stuff, Mateo's second football team, the new car, and pay a big lump off the mortgage. I'd lean on Ana's job too, because hospitals will need nurses for longer than mines need drivers, I think. I'd join whatever the union organises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the two years of warning give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Two years is enough to pay off a chunk of the mortgage and not much else. I can't become an electrician in two years with two kids and night shifts. I'd mostly be bracing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia and Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, but the short version. Dad's job is going to change, we've got savings, Mum's job is steady, nobody's going hungry. Sofia would ask a hundred follow-up questions. Mateo would ask if we can still get a dog.

S2.say: I'd say the government has failed if it lets this land with two years' notice and no plan. I'd push the union for income support for every miner right now, and I'd go to the march.
S2.think: If AI can do anything a person can, the loader drives itself and the eight remote chairs become one person watching. My two years of being good in the chair would count for nothing.
S2.do: Shelves the plan to build on the family's land, cuts extras such as a second football team and a new car, and pays a lump off the mortgage. Leans on his partner's nursing income and joins union action.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: I can't become an electrician in two years with two kids and night shifts.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture wipes out Diego's careful plan of becoming indispensable in the remote chair, and he sees that immediately. His money cushion lets him brace rather than panic. He quietly reorganises the family around his partner's nursing job, which he assumes is safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this right, so let's do it right: paid retraining, and a fund from the mining companies for the towns. I'd say it at the union and I'd write to our local member of parliament, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm forty-eight when it hits. I think it gives me a real chance to get a second trade before the loaders don't need anyone. My bet would be electrical, because somebody has to fix the robots, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrical apprenticeship part-time in the first year, nights or weekends, whatever the college offers. We'd still pay down the mortgage hard, but I'd keep the block of land, because in five years it might be worth more than the house. And I'd push the union for company-funded training, since I'm paying for mine myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with it. Doing something is better than lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. Two years is bracing, five years is a plan. I'd be fixing the machines that replaced me instead of watching them from the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said somebody has to fix the robots for a while. How long is a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. If the AI can do almost anything, maybe it fixes itself in the end. I'd just hope electrical buys me ten good years till the kids are grown.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do this right: paid retraining and a fund from the mining companies for the towns. I'd say it at the union and write to my local member of parliament.
S3.think: I'd be 48 when it hits, and five years gives me a real chance at a second trade. My bet would be electrical, because somebody has to fix the robots, at least for a while.
S3.do: Starts a part-time electrical apprenticeship in the first year while paying down the mortgage. Keeps the family's land, and presses the union and his MP for company-funded retraining.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, which he prefers to lying awake.
S3.quote: I'd be fixing the machines that replaced me instead of watching them from the kitchen.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Diego's worry into a plan, and he picks a trade with clear reasoning. He's honest that he doesn't know how long repair work would last if AGI can fix itself. Writing to his MP for the first time marks a step up in political action from the slower scenarios.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a crime if we waste it. The companies and the government should sit down now and plan which towns get what. I'd say it at work, and I'd probably help the union with that plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay. Ten years means I'm fifty-three, the mortgage is nearly done, Sofia's through university and Mateo's nearly there. I could finish an electrical trade without rushing and still work a few years at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical course over three or four years, steadily, while still on the loaders. We'd build on the block of land around year five, because a house we own outright is the best safety net I can think of. And we'd talk to Sofia about what to study, not to scare her, just to be smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for the town than for us. I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to pick something where people want a person, not just a result. She wants to be a vet, and I think that's a good one. Animals don't care how clever the computer is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young blokes who just started underground. They're twenty, they've got car loans and no trade. Ten years is their whole career up to the point where it disappears.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it and a crime if we waste it. Companies and government should sit down now and plan which towns get what, and I'd help the union with that.
S4.think: I think I'd be okay: at 53 the mortgage is nearly done and the kids are nearly through university. I could finish an electrical trade without rushing and still work a few years at it.
S4.do: Studies electrical over three or four years while still driving loaders. Plans to build on the family land around year five, and talks with his daughter about choosing studies that will last.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for the town and its young miners than for his own family.
S4.quote: Animals don't care how clever the computer is.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Diego is fairly confident about his own path and shifts his worry to young miners with car loans and no trade. The land he has held onto in every scenario becomes the centre of his plan here. His advice to his daughter is practical rather than fearful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to do anything except brace. What would help is income support that kicks in straight away, not after six months of forms, and free trade courses for anyone over forty. Make the mining companies pay into it, because they'd be saving a fortune on wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but robots underground could mean nobody dies in a rock fall again. I've lost a mate that way. I'd want to keep my job and I'd want that too, and I don't know how to hold both.

headlineQuote: I'd want to keep my job and I'd want that too, and I don't know how to hold both.
portrait: Diego Quinn is 43 and drives an underground loader at the Kestrel Deep gold mine, seven hundred metres down, with a partner who nurses and two kids. He has already done shifts in the surface remote-control chair and plans to make himself good at it, a careful, numbers-minded approach that works in the gentler scenarios. Fast AGI wipes that plan out and leaves him alarmed, while five or ten years turns into an electrical apprenticeship and a house built on land the family already owns. His politics are about rules that don't depend on a decent manager, and he's torn between his job and the lives robots might save underground.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to do anything except brace.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts straight away rather than after months of forms, and free trade courses for anyone over forty, paid for by the mining companies.
